en: The Sūtra on the Ten Dharmas of the Mahāyāna Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
There were five thousand great bhikṣus together with an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas.

At that time, within that great assembly of bodhisattvas, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Vimalanirmala-suvimala-ratnacandraprabharāja who was gathered among that great assembly of bodhisattvas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaviśuddhivimalaratnacandraprabharāja rose from his seat, left the lotus pedestal, and approached the Buddha. With his right shoulder bared and his right knee touching the ground, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"Bhagavān!
Regarding a Mahāyāna bhikṣu—one who dwells as a Mahāyāna bhikṣu—for what reason is he called a 'Mahāyāna bhikṣu'?
Furthermore, by what meaning is this Mahāyāna called 'Mahāyāna'?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaviśuddharatnacandraprabharāja, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Vimalaviśuddharatnacandraprabharāja!”
It is well that you are able to question the Tathāgata regarding this most profound and subtle meaning.
Son of good family, reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalavaiḍūryaprabhāśarājasaumya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It shall be as Your Honor has instructed!”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vimalaviśuddhavimalaratnacandraprabharāja, saying: "Good son,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he is said to dwell in the Great Vehicle."

What are these ten? They are: achieving right faith; achieving practice; achieving nature; delighting in the bodhicitta; delighting in the Dharma; delighting in contemplating the true Dharma; practicing the true Dharma and that which accords with the Dharma; remaining far removed from pride, self-conceit, and the like; being skillfully able to penetrate all subtle and esoteric teachings; and not delighting in the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes these ten dharmas is said to dwell in the Mahāyāna.
Good son!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes conduct that is free from flattery and crookedness and is gentle and harmonious, they are able to have faith in the unsurpassed enlightenment of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the Truly and Fully Awakened Ones; they are well able to have faith in the wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment; they believe that the *tathāgatagarbha* is neither interrupted nor eternal, neither subject to aging nor death, and is inexhaustible; and they also believe in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the characteristics of all-knowledge, the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).

Furthermore, he believes that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, cannot be consecrated, and he also believes in the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor excellencies, the halo, and other such dharmas.

Furthermore, they have faith in what is spoken by śrāvakas, or what is spoken by pratyekabuddhas, as well as what is spoken by bodhisattvas and others; they also have faith in the mundane and the supramundane. They further have faith in those who practice correctly, such as śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who follow the path of conformity; they also have faith in the ripening of the results of all roots of goodness, namely the most excellent and supreme fruits: whether as devas or deva-kings, or as humans or human kings.

Furthermore, one believes that the retribution for unwholesome karma is most inferior and evil, such that it is unpleasant to hear; it is undesirable, extremely heavy, and coarse, leading to rebirth in places such as the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.
Having thus gained faith, he abandons three things.
What are these three?
They are doubt, confusion, and indecisiveness.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these dharmas, they are said to possess right faith.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Faith is the supreme vehicle; by means of it, one attains perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, the wise revere and draw near to such qualities as faith.
Faith is the highest in the world; the faithful person lacks for nothing."
Therefore, the wise correctly cultivate qualities such as faith;
the son of good family who lacks faith does not give rise to any pure dharmas,
just as a scorched seed does not produce roots or sprouts.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplish all practices? Good son!”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva shaves off his hair and beard, dons the formal robes, and with profound and sincere faith, leaves home to enter the homeless life.

Having gone forth, he trains in the various practices of the Bodhisattva’s deportment and precepts, or the various practices of the Śrāvaka’s deportment and precepts, and also studies the practices of the Pratyekabuddha’s deportment and so forth.
In this way, whatever afflictions he habitually cultivates through his body, speech, and mind, all of them are extinguished together.
Among these, what are the afflictions habitually cultivated by means of the body?

What are called killing, stealing, covetousness, and sexual misconduct; wielding weapons, staves, tiles, or stones; being stingy toward others; moving one's hands and feet; and acts such as fleeing or running away—these are termed the afflictions shared with the body.
Among these, what are the afflictions commonly practiced through the gateway of speech?
They are namely: lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech—constantly uttering evil words and slandering the profound scriptures.
To spread one's ill repute among elders and those practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) is called the mental habituation to afflictions through speech.
Among these, what is the mental habituation to afflictions belonging to the mind?

That is to say: stinginess and greed, false views, jealousy, delighting in fame and profit; pride in one’s kin, pride in one’s caste, pride in youth, pride in being free from illness, pride in longevity and extensive learning, and pride in one’s reflections; thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill-will, and evil thoughts; thoughts of relatives, and thoughts of one’s native land; thoughts of food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and various necessities; attachment to dwellings, vehicles, and couches; attachment to various foods and drinks, wives, children, and grandchildren; engagement in plowing, farming, and the management of slaves and servants; matters concerning money, grain, and stores; and even attachment to all manner of implements and utensils.

Having thus become stingy and attached, if he loses even a single item among those things he has spoken of, he immediately gives rise to sorrow, suffering, affliction, and delusive conceptualizations.
Once he has thus distanced his mind from the moisture of craving, he gives rise to reflection.
"Good son!
To speak briefly, mental karma is like the revolving wheel of the world; therefore, it is said that mental karma is identical to habitual tendencies and afflictions.

Having thus become free from the habitual tendencies and afflictions associated with the karma of body, speech, and mind, he conceives the thought of a preceptor toward his teacher (upādhyāya), the thought of a teacher toward his preceptor (ācārya), and a sense of earnest reverence toward his fellow practitioners of the holy life, whether they be old or young."
Remaining alone in a secluded place, he reflects thus: "I ought not to act in such a way;

I have undertaken these practices for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, and for the sake of establishing all sentient beings in tranquility, discipline, and meditative concentration."
However, I myself have not yet been tamed, my faculties have not been concealed, and I have not attained tranquility.

I must certainly practice the right conduct so that whoever sees me will surely attain the state of being tamed; furthermore, I shall follow the subtle and equal teachings of all Buddhas and cause the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others to rejoice.
"Good son! This is called the shame of a bodhisattva.
He reflects in this way:"

"May no one—whether monastic or lay—find fault with me regarding any of my modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), namely: in the practice of the precepts, in improper conduct, or in what is observed of my physical appearance, my deportment, my requisites, or my manner of sustaining life."
Having thus felt shame and remorse, they contemplate the dharmas such as the observance of precepts during the six periods of the day and night.
Having properly observed the precepts, they are free from further doubt or regret, causing them to enter and abide within the Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata without cessation.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s sense of shame. Good son!"
"This is called a bodhisattva’s accomplishment of such practices.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The practices of all Buddhas, as well as those of the śrāvaka disciples, are rooted in [this]."
Therefore, the wise cultivate this, practicing with constant firmness.
The great wisdom of all Bodhisattvas consists in performing fearless deeds;
they cause others to realize the stainless path, which is praised by all Buddhas.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of nature?

Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva’s nature is perfected, they have little desire, anger, or delusion; they are without envy, stinginess, or vexation; they do not speak coarse words; they do not harbor ill will or engage in frivolous play; they are not fickle or restless, but are harmonious, gentle, and worthy of being approached. By their very nature, they are able to accomplish supreme and wondrous offerings to serve all Buddhas—namely, by bestowing upon others material resources such as provisions, and by fully perfecting the giving of hands, feet, head, eyes, and so forth.”
If one sees the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, upon seeing them, one immediately gives rise to a mind of reverence and joy.
Good son! This is what is called the perfection of the bodhisattva’s nature.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“From smoke one knows fire; By the mandarin duck, water is revealed.
Likewise, by their mutual characteristics, The Bodhisattva of great renown is known.”
Gentle and free from guile, having abandoned stinginess and envy,
and feeling compassion for all beings— such a one is called a bodhisattva.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s joy and delight in the bodhicitta?

If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, at the time when the nature of his being slightly gives rise to the bodhicitta, encounters Buddhas, bodhisattvas, or śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who teach, exhort, and inspire him to generate the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—this is called the mark of the initial arousal of the bodhicitta characterized by joy and delight.”
Having heard of bodhi and the merits of bodhi, they immediately resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called the second sign of delighting in bodhi.

When that bodhisattva sees that sentient beings have no one to rescue or protect them, no place of refuge, are solitary and without anyone to deliver them, lacking shelter, lacking a home, and lacking an island, he immediately gives rise to a heart of compassion.
Having thus resolved his mind, he forms this thought:
"I shall now act as a protector, a refuge, a deliverer, a shelter, and an island for all sentient beings."
For the sake of those causes and conditions, one generates the mind of unsurpassed bodhi; this is called the third joyful generation of the bodhicitta.

If one sees a Tathāgata, or a Bodhisattva, Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or others who have fulfilled all practices, and upon seeing them, joy arises in the heart, leading to a mind of love, respect, and tranquility, then by means of these causes and conditions, one generates the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called the fourth generation of the bodhicitta.

For the sake of the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings, that bodhisattva practices generosity, maintains ethical discipline, cultivates patience, exerts diligence, practices meditative concentration, and develops right wisdom.
"How does a bodhisattva practice generosity? It is said: to those who need drink, he gives drink;

to those who need food, he gives food; to those who need a vehicle, he provides a vehicle; to those who need beds, couches, or bedding, he provides beds, couches, bedding, and so forth; to those who need clothing, he gives clothing; to those who need gold, silver, jeweled crowns, bracelets, armlets, and other various ornaments—even up to his own skin and flesh—he bestows them to benefit and nourish sentient beings."
Having practiced giving in this manner, he dedicates that gift toward the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; although he gives, he does not give rise to thoughts of pride or the like.
“What is the upholding of precepts?

It is the accomplishment of the actions of body, speech, and mind; having abandoned such actions of body, speech, and mind, one is skillfully detached from them, guarded against them, unimpeded, and untainted, purely and without admixture, upholding the prohibitive precepts.”

However, while observing the precepts, they dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; thus, although they practice the observance of the precepts, they do not give rise to thoughts of pride or the like. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva cultivate patience?

Whether reviled and abused, imprisoned and bound, or subjected to mutilation and flogging—whether by monastics or laypeople—they are able to endure and tolerate it, without giving rise to any habitual afflictions or the like.
Having thus cultivated patience, he dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; although he cultivates patience, he does not give rise to thoughts of pride or the like.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva arouse the mind of diligence?
He forms this thought:”

"Just as the realm of space is immeasurable and boundless, so too is the realm of sentient beings immeasurable and boundless; yet, regarding this realm of sentient beings, I alone am without a second, and I shall establish them all within the realm of nirvana without remainder."
For this reason, on account of those causes and conditions, he exerts diligence and does not separate his body from the contemplation of mindfulness of the body;
having contemplated the body, he contemplates feelings; having contemplated feelings, he contemplates the mind and mental formations;
having contemplated the mind and mental formations, he contemplates all phenomena in accordance with reality.

Having thus recollected and observed them well, he generates desire, exerts effort, applies diligence, upholds the mind, and practices with right application (*samyak-pratipatti*) so that unarisen unwholesome and evil dharmas do not arise;
he generates desire, exerts effort, applies diligence, maintains a straightforward mind, and practices with right application so that unarisen wholesome dharmas may arise;
and he generates desire, exerts effort, applies diligence, upholds the mind, and practices with right application so that arisen unwholesome dharmas may be extinguished.

In order that all wholesome states already arisen may endure for a long time and further increase, one arouses desire, exerts effort, applies diligence, sustains the mind, and practices right conduct.
Having aroused diligence, he brings about the first factor of the bases of psychic power; likewise, he brings about the second, the third, and even the fourth factor of the bases of psychic power.

Having accomplished the factors of mastery (*vaśitā*), he is able to remain for an eon or slightly less than an eon, or he may fully practice so as to fulfill the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Having thus aroused vigor, he dedicates that vigor toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Although he exerts such diligence, his mind does not give rise to arrogance.
"Good son! How does a bodhisattva contemplate the practice of meditative concentration?"

It is the departure from desire, the cessation of desire, the stilling of desire; it does not rely on the internal, nor on the external; it does not rely on form, nor on feeling, perception, or consciousness; it does not rely on the realms of desire, form, or formlessness; it does not rely on emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; it does not rely on the mundane or the supramundane; and it does not rely on generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and so forth.
"Good son!
Briefly stated, all conceptualizations of existence and their fetters are called dhyāna.

One thus cultivates these various dhyānas, yet dedicates that dhyāna toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Although one contemplates and cultivates this dhyāna, one does not give rise to a mind of pride or the like."
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva cultivate wisdom?
He forms this thought:”
"I shall cause immeasurable and boundless realms of sentient beings to enter nirvāṇa, yet not a single sentient being enters nirvāṇa. Why is this?
As the Buddha has taught regarding all dharmas: they are without self, without sentient beings, without life, without a soul, and without a person (pudgala).
Thus one cultivates the wisdom of insight, yet that wisdom is dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Although one contemplates and cultivates prajñā, one does not give rise to thoughts of conceit or the like.
“Good son!
Thus does a bodhisattva mahāsattva delight in the bodhicitta.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Just as a mani jewel, revealed within a treasury of gems,
becomes twice as bright in its natural color through the application of effort by a master;
having perfected such a nature, one seeks the mind of right enlightenment."
"Since both extremes are stilled, Māra finds no opportunity.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva achieve the accomplishment of delighting in the Dharma?"
"Noble son!

If a bodhisattva is by nature fond of the Dharma, delights in the Dharma, and loves the Dharma, then upon seeing any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, he is able to offer them all their requisites, life-sustaining implements, food, drink, and other such necessities."
Having gathered all the worldly resources available—such as roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits—he gives them to all sentient beings.

He causes those who uphold the Dharma to go and pay their respects, to bow with palms joined, and upon receiving them, he welcomes them with profound reverence. Wherever there is doubt in his mind, he inquires about the correct meaning;
thus, the upholder of the Dharma is well able to explain the meanings according to what he has heard.
Toward those who hear the Dharma, they conceive the notion that they are the World-Honored One, the notion that they are spiritual friends, and the notion that they are like the oceans of the world;
they conceive the notion that they are preceptors and the notion that they are ācāryas;
and toward those who have long been lost in the wilderness of the world during times when guidance is absent amidst hardships, they conceive the notion of being seekers as they search for them.
Because the long-dwelling ignorant have had their eyes closed by darkness, he causes them to give rise to the thought of awakening;
because they have fallen and sunk into the mud of worldly afflictions, he causes them to give rise to the thought of being rescued and pulled out;
because they have long lost the correct path, he acts as their guide, causing them to give rise to the thought of a guide.
Because they have long lain prostrate within the prison of the world and are able to release it, they conceive the thought of being a liberator;
because they have long been afflicted by illness and provide medical treatment, they conceive the thought of being a skilled physician;
and because the fire of afflictions has scorched and extinguished their bodies, causing them to abide in cessation, they conceive the thought of being a great cloud and rain.

For the sake of the Dharma and because it is the cause of the Dharma, he is able to endure cold and heat, wind and rain, mosquitoes and gadflies; he likewise endures hunger and thirst. Furthermore, even when seeing others receiving the retribution of pleasure, he does not give rise to a mind that longs for such pleasure.
Yet he forms this thought:
"I alone in the world enjoy happiness, for I am able to hear the True Dharma.
On account of this matter, and by reason of that cause and condition, he does not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, or resentment.
Having thus become free from sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, he gives rise to this thought:
"Because I am capable of bearing even a single verse of the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, I shall dwell in the Avīci Hell for one kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa."

Having thus attained a mind free from weariness, they naturally cease all conditioned activities and realize all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); furthermore, they cause those Buddha-qualities not yet attained to be swiftly acquired.
“Good son! For this reason, a bodhisattva is said to be ‘delightfully attached to all dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Those of great wisdom who delight in all dharmas become the children of the Buddhas;
they draw near to the true and wondrous Dharma without ever becoming weary.
With a reverent mind they seek the true Dharma—these children of the Buddha with their profound resolve.”
"And by recollecting them with the mind, one also manifests right and wondrous conduct. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva correctly contemplate all phenomena?"
"Good son! If a bodhisattva contemplates in this way:
'All dharmas are like illusions, for they delude ordinary beings;'"
All phenomena are like dreams, because they are not real;
all phenomena are like the moon in water, because they are not substantial entities;
all phenomena are like echoes, because they are not sentient beings.
All dharmas are like shadows, for they are reckoned as products of deluded conceptualization;
all dharmas are like echoes, for they arise, perish, and disintegrate.
All dharmas arise, perish, and disintegrate, for they are formed through the conjunction of conditions and designations.
All dharmas are fundamentally unborn and non-transmigrating, for they share the same essence as true suchness;
all dharmas are non-extinguished, for they are fundamentally unborn;
all dharmas are without action, for there is no agent.
All phenomena are like space, because they cannot be defiled;
all phenomena are eternally quiescent, because their nature is undefiled;
all phenomena are stainless, because they are free from all stains.
The nature of all phenomena is extinguished, for they are free from afflictions.
All phenomena are non-material, for they cannot be seen;
all phenomena are beyond the sphere of the mind, for they lack intrinsic nature.
All dharmas do not abide, because they extinguish all poisons;
all dharmas cannot be sought, because they extinguish the mind of love and hatred;
all dharmas are without attachment, because they are free from the realm of afflictions.
All dharmas are like venomous snakes because they are devoid of skillful means;
all dharmas are like plantain trees because they lack solidity;
all dharmas are like bubbles on water because their essential nature is weak.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva contemplates in this manner, it is called the correct contemplation of all dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are like illusions, deluding the ignorant and the confused;
they are as empty and precarious as dreams—hold this view, all of you.
Phenomena are like the moon reflected in water, and likewise like echoes and such things."
“Furthermore, like reflections and the like, the wise do not perceive them. “Good son,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the Dharma and accord with the Dharma?”
“Good son!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the impermanence of form yet does not become weary of or detached from form;

having sought to realize the Dharma, they assist the dharma-dhātu with right knowledge, entering through skillful contemplation by employing the equal Dharma; and they skillfully maintain those various marks, skillfully reflecting upon them, and skillfully memorizing them.”

Having been thus instructed regarding these signs, and having properly maintained, cultivated, and mastered them, he spontaneously practices the conduct that is equal to the dharma-realm; he contemplates sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent, yet he does not feel weary of or seek to renounce consciousness and the other aggregates.
Having entered the Dharma-realm, one is assisted by right wisdom.

One skillfully contemplates and penetrates the dharmas that are equal to the Dharma-realm, and likewise notes their characteristics. Having skillfully maintained, skillfully cultivated, and skillfully noted them, one spontaneously enters the practice of equality with the Dharma-realm; as it is with impermanence, so it is with suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Having contemplated the impermanence of form, he does not give rise to fear, terror, or the like regarding form.
Why is this? Form arises from false imagination and inversion, yet he knows it as it truly is.
One contemplates that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; even regarding consciousness, one does not feel fear, dread, or alarm.
Why is this? Because consciousness arises from false imagination and inversion, yet one knows it as it truly is.
"Good son!
It is like a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s disciple who creates various illusory phenomena, such as elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry."
Having seen this, that wise person does not give rise to fear, alarm, or the like. Why is this?
Because they know it as it truly is: that it is a creation of a magician, unreal, and never produced through falsehood.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: having contemplated that form (*rūpa*) is impermanent, they do not give rise to fear, terror, or the like regarding form.

Why is this? Because form arises from false conceptualization and inversion; yet they know it as it truly is. Having contemplated that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are impermanent, they likewise do not give rise to fear, terror, or the like regarding consciousness.
"Why is this? Because consciousness arises from deluded conceptualization and inversion; yet, one knows it as it truly is.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhāśrī-viśuddharatnacandraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva contemplates all forms as impermanent, yet does not become weary of or detached from form?
And having realized the dharma-realm, how do they use right wisdom to contemplate and enter the dharmas that assist the dharma-realm?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vimalaviśuddhivairocanaratnacandraprabharāja, saying: "Good son,
I shall now explain a parable for you in detail."
"Good son!

It is like a wise man who constantly serves various poisons, yet he maintains them well, covers them well, and guards them well; having conceived the notion of 'self,' he uses them to trade for various ornaments and articles, yet he does not consume those poisons, lest he lose his livelihood because of this matter."
The Bodhisattva is also like this: his mind is directed toward nirvāṇa, moistened by the direction toward nirvāṇa, inclined toward nirvāṇa, and drawing near to nirvāṇa;
yet he does not realize that nirvāṇa.
For what reason?
Lest I, because of this matter, should fall back from my bodhisattva practice.
"O son of good family!

For example, suppose there is a person who serves the fire deity, and that person day and night makes offerings of incense, flowers, and so forth, honoring, respecting, praising, and attending upon it; yet that person does not form this thought:
"Having served the fire with offerings, honor, respect, praise, and attendance, I shall now take hold of it with both hands."
Why is this? "May I not, because of this matter, experience suffering in my body or affliction in my mind.
In this way, the bodhisattva directs his mind toward nirvāṇa, moistens himself toward nirvāṇa, inclines toward nirvāṇa, and even grasps at nirvāṇa; yet, he does not realize nirvāṇa.
"Why is this? Lest I, because of this matter, should fall back from my bodhisattva practice.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhāśuddharatnacandraprabharāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the intent of what the World-Honored One has said, a bodhisattva should dwell in the world.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Son of good family,
a bodhisattva should dwell in the world."
He asked: "World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva dwell in the world without being defiled by the various afflictions of the world?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son! For this purpose, I shall briefly provide a single analogy."
Good son!

It is like a person skilled in incantations who, by the power of great mantras, plays with various evil poisons, venomous snakes, and the like; yet that person does not have their life-force severed because of these things.
Why is this? It is because that person has skillfully mastered the power of incantations.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: though he acts within the world and dwells within the world, once established therein, by the power of the incantation of great wisdom and skillful means, he dwells and sports among the venomous snakes of all afflictions, even playing with them while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
A bodhisattva does not retreat from awakening on account of such matters.
Why is this? Because they have accomplished the power of the mantra of great wisdom and skillful means.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalavaiḍūryaśuddharatnacandraprabharāja said:
“World-Honored One!
How rare, how rare!”
Those bodhisattvas are able to refrain from realizing nirvana, yet they are not defiled by the poisons of worldly afflictions.
World-Honored One!
I now take refuge in these great bodhisattvas.
“World-Honored One!
These sentient beings, having accomplished various roots of goodness, upon hearing this Dharma, give rise to a single heart of joy.
World-Honored One!”
"Those sons and daughters of good family have already been prophesied by all the Buddhas:
'If they are able to hear this Dharma-gate.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus who had not yet realized the outflow-free state attained liberation.

Having attained liberation, they immediately rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These bodhisattvas are worthy of reverence and worship.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Homage to those of great wisdom; homage to those who have attained fearlessness;
homage to those with purified eyes; homage to the true children of the Buddha.
Because of their skillful means and their supreme, wondrous wisdom, [they are honored].
The Bodhisattva of great renown is able to transcend the stages of the two vehicles.
Knowing the aggregates as they truly are— namely, consciousness and its arising and ceasing—
and seeing that the world looks up with longing, he does not realize nirvana.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abandon pride and overweening pride? Good son!”

Pride (*māna*) is that which thinks "I am superior" on account of one's self, or one's family, or one's clan, or one's physical appearance, or other matters such as wealth and resources like gold and silver, or the fourfold army consisting of elephants, cavalry, infantry, and chariots; any such state of mind characterized by loftiness or inferiority is called pride.

One who possesses *māna* (pride) gives rise to the conceit of "I am superior" based on their family, clan, physical appearance, and so forth; or based on gold, silver, wealth, granaries, or the fourfold army consisting of elephants, cavalry, infantry, and chariots. Such mental delight and haughty disposition, which does not humble others, is called *adhimāna* (overweening pride).
"When a bodhisattva relinquishes such dharmas as these, it is called being free from pride and overweening pride.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Free from pride and overweening pride, Always mindful with a heart of compassion,"
"Furthermore, always harboring a compassionate heart, constantly fearing the world,
always subsisting by begging for food, and skillfully expounding the benefits for humans and devas. "Good son!"
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skill in secret language?
Son of good family,

if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding the secret teachings within the various profound sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, does not grasp them according to their literal expression— this is what constitutes the secret teaching.
"The Tathāgata’s prediction regarding the śrāvakas attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is not as it was spoken.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"I am suffering from back pain and cannot follow the instructions to fetch [the medicine]. I am old, infirm, and decrepit; go and seek one for me. My attendant did not follow the instructions to fetch it. Maudgalyāyana, go to Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, and fetch some excellent medicines, but you must not take them exactly as they were described."
When the Tathāgata debated with various non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others regarding their various arts, one should not accept it as it was stated.

As for the matter of the *khadira* thorn piercing the Tathāgata’s foot, this should not be accepted according to what was said. Devadatta was a long-standing persecutor and enemy of the Tathāgata; one should not accept [his words] merely according to what he said.
When the Tathāgata entered the brahmin village of Śālīya and emerged with an empty bowl, one should not accept it as being true according to what was said.
As for the slanders of Ciñcā and Sundarī against the Buddha, one should not accept them as being true according to what was said.
"The Brahmin Vīrajā of the country of Sunāra invited the Buddha to eat barley; this, too, should not be accepted as you have described.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhavimalasupariśuddharatnacandraprabharāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“World-Honored One, why do you prophesy that all śrāvakas shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
"I record that those śrāvakas who have attained the unsurpassed, right, true, and complete path do so because they possess the [buddha-]nature.
The Bodhisattva Vimalanirbhāsaratnacandraprabharāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that those śrāvakas who have exhausted all outflows and severed the habitual tendencies of afflictions might, if they possess the [bodhisattva] nature, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said:
"Good son!..."
I shall now provide an analogy.

Suppose there is a son of a consecrated universal monarch (cakravartin) who wishes to learn all the various arts and crafts; yet he possesses middling faculties rather than sharp faculties. He should learn later what ought to be learned first, and learn first what ought to be learned later.
"Good son! What do you think?
On account of this matter, could one say that he is not a prince?"
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One!"
"This is the son of a virtuous king. "Good son!

It is the same for the bodhisattva: because he has already perfected the faculty of middling capacity, he cultivates the gateway of the path; first he eliminates all afflictive obstructions, and subsequently he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Good son, what do you think?
Could it be said on account of this matter that he has not attained perfect enlightenment?”
He replied:
“World-Honored One!

Among the multitudes of sentient beings—whether gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, humans, devas, or asuras—I see none who would say that you have not attained perfect enlightenment, with the sole exception of the icchantikas.”
The Buddha said,
"Good son, listen further to another parable."
"Good son!
Does a bodhisattva of the tenth stage sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in order to sever all afflictions, or not?"
He replied:
"World-Honored One,
because they have been severed."
“Good son, what do you think? Could he not,
by means of this, attain perfect enlightenment?”
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
This is called accomplishment.”
The Buddha said, "Good son,
it is just like this."
The Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhā-viśuddha-ratnacandraprabharāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why did you say to the bhikṣu Ānanda:”
"I am suffering from back pain," [he said].
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Out of compassion for sentient beings of future generations, I have spoken these words.
Even the Buddhas with adamantine bodies suffer from back pain; how much more so those others?”
Yet those foolish sentient beings accept [his words] according to his teaching; having ruined themselves, they also ruin others.
"I am decrepit, aged, and infirm; seek for me an attendant."

"Good son! These words of mine are also spoken for the sake of future generations. After my parinirvāṇa, there will be no disciples in the world to come; therefore, I speak of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are decayed, aged, and afflicted by illness. It is because of this—that they, having been granted permission by the Buddha, harbor no sense of shame regarding the physical body they have received as their attendant—that I say the Tathāgata is decayed, aged, and afflicted by illness."
“World-Honored One!
How can it be that you say, ‘Maudgalyāyana, go to the great physician-king Jīvaka and fetch some medicine’?”

“Good son! These words of mine were also spoken for the sake of future generations, so that my śrāvakas, having the necessary medicines and knowing they have the Buddha’s permission, shall never lack for them.”
It was for this reason that the Tathāgata spoke thus.

Those foolish sentient beings grasp what has been said [literally]. The Tathāgata is one who has transcended the body of affliction. When the monk Maudgalyāyana went to Jīvaka’s place, he neither prostrated nor showed respect; because of his hasty intention, having heard [the diagnosis], he spoke of the medicine in a hurried manner.
“Good son!
This also describes the afflictions of the various desires and so forth; even those who have realized and seen the Dharma forget them, let alone ordinary worldlings.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by 'what is grasped'?
[The claim that] 'the Tathāgata disputed with various non-Buddhists, such as the Nirgranthas, over their various arts.
I spoke these words for the sake of sentient beings of future generations; if even the Tathāgata has enemies, how much more so should we?"
However, those foolish sentient beings speak according to their literal grasping, saying that the Tathāgata has enemies and the like.

Even a Cakravartin King, by virtue of his subtle roots of goodness, is free from all such afflictions; how much more so the Tathāgata, who has perfected the treasury of all merits—how could he be subject to such grasping?

When the khatvāṅga thorn pierced the Tathāgata’s foot, the Tathāgata likewise spoke of past karmic retribution; if even the Tathāgata must undergo the retribution of past karma, how much more so for other ordinary persons?
For this reason, and due to those causes and conditions, sentient beings are shown to commit evil karma;
for this purpose, the matter of the retribution of that karma is demonstrated.
"Yet those foolish sentient beings perceive it as it truly is, such that the *khatvāṅga* thorns pierce the Tathāgata’s feet.
"World-Honored One,
how can it be so perceived?"
“Devadatta is a spiritual friend, yet he is also an enemy who has been close to the Tathāgata for a long time.
“Good son! [It is so.]”
If it were not for the spiritual friend Devadatta, the merits and virtues of the Tathāgata and all Buddhas would not have been manifested. Good son!
It is for this reason that the spiritual friend Devadatta contended with the Tathāgata in matters such as skillful arts and moral conduct, and displayed acts such as those of an enemy.
However, this is to manifest the merit of the Tathāgata’s various great wisdoms. Good son!

If Devadatta, having received the king’s command, were to loose the great elephant Dhanapāla among the great assembly, that elephant would have been capable of harming the Tathāgata had he approached; yet, by the power of the Tathāgata, it was subdued and well-tamed.

At that time, when the immeasurable multitude of people saw that the elephant had been tamed, they gave rise to a sense of rare wonder and immediately took refuge in the Three Jewels—namely, the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel. This is called the characteristic of Devadatta as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
However, there are foolish people who take things according to what is said, thinking that Devadatta was an enemy of the Tathāgata.

Although Devadatta manifested the conduct of a bodhisattva for five hundred lifetimes, and what he displayed was intended to reveal the Tathāgata’s virtue and morality, ignorant sentient beings followed his teachings literally, taking him to be an enemy and a harmer of the Tathāgata. Because of these causes and conditions, they abandoned their bodies and fell into the Avīci Hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm.
Why is this? Good son!

Devadatta has well accumulated various practices and well accumulated various roots of goodness. Having made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, he has planted roots of goodness and Mahāyāna practices under those Buddhas. He has correctly trained in bodhi, turned toward bodhi, and does not retreat from great bodhi; he is close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Because these sentient beings give rise predominantly to evil, after their lives end, they fall into the Avīci Hell, among hungry ghosts, or among animals, where they undergo various sufferings in succession.
"Good son! What is that which is grasped? It is:
'The Tathāgata has entered the brahmin village of Śālīya.'"
"Good son! Out of compassion for future generations, I have practiced and demonstrated this teaching. Why is this?"
There is no karmic retribution that can confront the Tathāgata;

however, for the sake of protecting future generations, should any bhikṣus who beg for alms enter villages, towns, cities, or royal capitals, they may fail to obtain food due to the power of their meager merit.
At that time, he correctly recollected me, thinking:
"That Buddha, the World-Honored One, who is fully endowed with all merits, went forth with an empty bowl; how much more so should we, whose roots of goodness are so slight?"
"For this reason, our minds should not give rise to despondency.
It was for this purpose that the Tathāgata entered the village with an empty bowl and came out.
Furthermore, he spoke these words:
"One should not accept what is said [when it is claimed]: 'The Māra Pāpīyān has disciplined the brahmins so that they will not provide food for the Tathāgata. Why is this? "
Māra did not possess such supernatural power as to be able to obstruct the Tathāgata’s meal.
At that time, by the supernatural power of all the Buddhas, Māra caused the brahmins and householders in various places to be punished; yet the Tathāgata remained entirely without fault.
In order to manifest for those sentient beings, the Tathāgata displayed such skillful means and other deeds.
At that time, after the Tathāgata and his śrāvaka disciples had fasted, Māra and his followers, along with various other devas, observed the Tathāgata’s mind, thinking:
"Is this śramaṇa Gautama and his śrāvaka disciples afflicted by distress?"

Having thus contemplated the Tathāgata and his disciples throughout the day, and being free from any thoughts of resentment, regret, or distress, he remained neither elated nor dejected, as he was before, so too thereafter.
At that time, seven thousand sons of the gods within that assembly, their hearts filled with joy, took refuge in the Buddha.
The Tathāgata skillfully transformed them by preaching the sublime Dharma; having heard the Dharma, they attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding the teachings of the Tathāgata.
"In this way, the Tathāgata contemplates matters of future lives; the Buddha has no karmic retribution.
"World-Honored One!
How can this be accepted?"
"Cañcā, Sundarī, and others placed wooden vessels upon their bellies and slandered the Tathāgata. He replied,
"O son of good family!
The Tathāgata has no affliction of karmic retribution.
Having perfected all supernatural powers, the Tathāgata causes Cañcā and Sundarī to pass through worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers and places them securely there.
However, it is by the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means that he manifests such matters as karmic retribution and various slanders.
Among those who have gone forth within my Dharma, some may be falsely slandered; having heard such slander, they may give rise to sorrow, anxiety, doubt, and regret.
He spoke thus:
"If even the Tathāgata, who has perfected all pure dharmas, was slandered face-to-face, how much more so should we not be slandered?"
At that time, he endured all those slanders and practiced the pure brahmacarya without falling back.

As for Ciñcā Mānavikā and Sundarī, dragged by their own evil karma, they even slandered the Tathāgata within their dreams; having so slandered him, they cast off their bodies and fell into the miserable realms.
If the Tathāgata knows that a being is capable of being saved, he shall save them. Why is this?
Because there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata would abandon.
“World-Honored One!
How can it be accepted that ‘the Tathāgata,
having been invited for a three-month retreat by the brahmin Verañjā in the kingdom of Uruvelā, ate nothing but barley’?”
He replied: “The Tathāgata knew that although the brahmins and householders had invited him, they would not provide the offerings.
Knowing this, the Tathāgata went there nonetheless.”

Why is this? As for those five hundred horses, they were all originally monks who ate barley alongside the Tathāgata and his assembly of bhikṣus. They had all practiced the bodhisattva path and attended upon the Buddhas of the past; however, because they encountered evil associates, they committed various unwholesome deeds and were consequently reborn among animals. The one who was able to tame and instruct these five hundred horses is named Bodhisattva Vajragarbha; by the power of his vows, he was born in that place.
These horses were inspired to resolve upon bodhicitta by the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha; for the sake of transforming them, they were born in that place.
By the power of that horse-tamer, all those horses remembered their former lives, and their bodhicitta was manifested.
"Good son!

Out of compassion for those five hundred horses, the Tathāgata went to that place to tame the horse trainer. He divided the barley in half, giving one portion to the Buddha, and he also divided all the barley belonging to the five hundred horses in half, giving one portion to the bhikṣus."
By means of the horses' own sounds, that horse trainer caused those five hundred horses to repent their transgressions and perform prostrations to the Buddha and the Sangha.

Then, after those three proclamations had been made, those horses cast off their bodies and were reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven; having been born there among the devas, they further made offerings to the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata skillfully taught and transformed them with the Dharma; having heard the Dharma, they immediately became non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As for those five hundred horses who were tamed and protected by him, the Tathāgata also prophesied that they would become *pratyekabuddhas*, named "Well-Tamed Mind" (*Suvinitacitta*).
Furthermore, son of good family!
There is no compassion of the Tathāgata that is incomplete or not constant.
Son of good family!

Even if the Tathāgata were to eat earth, wood, tiles, stones, and the like, there would be no such flavors or superior flavors within this trichiliocosm as those found in that earth, wood, tile, stone, and so forth.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses the mark of a Great Man, which consists of the most sublime flavor among all flavors.
O son of good family!
For this reason, you should understand it thus: all foods of the Tathāgata are of the most sublime flavor.
Son of good family!
The bhikṣu Ānanda gave rise to a heart of compassion, thinking: "The Tathāgata renounced the position of a Wheel-Turning King, yet now he eats barley."
The Tathāgata, having known Ānanda’s mind, gave him a single grain of barley and said to Ānanda:
"Do you know what this tastes like?
Having eaten it, he was struck by a sense of wonder and extraordinary marvel, and said to me:
“World-Honored One!
I was born and raised in a royal family, yet I have never before tasted such a supreme flavor.
By the power of this supreme flavor, the bhikṣu Ānanda experienced sublime and wondrous joy for seven days and no longer ate.
"Good son!
For this reason, you should understand it thus: the Tathāgata has no karmic retribution for actions.

If there are sentient beings who purely uphold the various precepts—whether they be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas—and do not follow through with offerings as previously requested, the Tathāgata demonstrates these matters of karmic retribution for them in order to speak what is not false."

“Good son! You should observe that among all the dharmas of the Tathāgata’s various bodies, there is that which the brahmin invited the Tathāgata to establish, yet the Tathāgata did not do so; nevertheless, the Tathāgata also taught him so that he would not fall back.”
However, son of good family!
Regarding those five hundred bhikṣus whom the Tathāgata has prophesied shall not fall back—
furthermore, son of good family!

Among those five hundred bhikṣus who were observing the summer retreat together with the Tathāgata, there were forty bhikṣus who frequently dwelt upon the fetters of desire. When they thought of obtaining fine food, their thoughts of desire and their sensual cravings would flare up; however, because of the condition of receiving coarse food, their thoughts of desire and sensual cravings became faint.
Once it had subsided, he attained the fruit of Arhatship after seven days and seven nights.
"Good son! If one can understand the words spoken by the Tathāgata in this way, that is called correct understanding."
“Good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes such as this is said to be skillful in understanding the secret teachings spoken by the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The teachings spoken in a gradual manner, as well as those taught all at once—
these the bodhisattvas of great wisdom understand correctly through their secrets;
they are skilled in various esoteric expressions and in the teachings spoken as a response to Śāriputra.”
"Thoroughly penetrating the teaching of the True Dharma, as spoken by all Buddhas. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva not take delight in the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"
"Good son!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, even by means of the sufferings of hell or the various heavy evils endured by hungry ghosts, animals, and so forth, does not take pleasure in seeking the nirvāṇa of a śrāvaka."
Furthermore, they do not contemplate how to attain a mind of world-weariness and renunciation so as to swiftly achieve mastery;
nor do they seek few desires and few activities, nor do they seek the causal practices of few desires and few activities.
Regarding those sentient beings whom he sees practicing various wholesome deeds, the Bodhisattva assists them so that they may achieve success.
Furthermore, he exhorts all sentient beings to praise, correctly explain, and correctly demonstrate [the path], directing them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has accomplished such merits as these, he takes no delight in the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Transforming sentient beings without weariness, Not retreating from bodhi,
Holding the mind like the king of mountains, Practicing the dharma of universal loving-kindness. At that time,
the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhāśuddharatnacandrarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has already explained all dharmas, and it is said that a bodhisattva who has accomplished these dharmas is called one who dwells in the Mahāyāna.
Yet, the Tathāgata has not yet explained for what reason it is called the ‘Mahāyāna.’”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vimalaviśuddharatnacandraprabharāja, saying:
"Good son, I now question you; speak according to your own understanding."
"Good son! What do you think?
As for the path traveled by a wheel-turning sage king together with his fourfold army, how is that path described?"
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is called the Royal Path; it is also called the Great Path, the Path of Fearlessness, the Unobstructed Path, and the Path of Quiescence.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son, the Tathāgata is also like this."

Whatever vehicle one mounts to reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that vehicle is called the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), the Superior Vehicle, the Wondrous Vehicle, the Subtle and Wondrous Vehicle, the Victorious Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Vehicle Without Evil, the Peerless Vehicle, the Unequaled Vehicle, and the Vehicle Equal to the Unequaled.
"Good son!
For this reason, it is called the Mahāyāna.
He replied:
“Excellent, Great Vehicle!
World-Honored One!”
“Excellent!
The Mahāyāna!
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas had this thought:
"This ascetic Gautama has transcended my domain, and he has enabled others as well to transcend their domains.
If I were to assemble the fourfold army and go together to harass and disturb him, it would be because I have not yet taught this Dharma; therefore, I shall go to where the ascetic Gautama is."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān led his fourfold army to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in the great city of Rājagṛha.
Then, the Bodhisattva Vimalanirmalavimalaratnacandraprabharāja saw from afar that Māra Pāpīyān was leading his fourfold army, intending to create obstacles for this Dharma teaching.
Having seen this, he performed such a supernatural power—having manifested this power, the Māra Pāpīyān went to the crossroads and thoroughfares of the great city of Rājagṛha and uttered these words:
"All of you, go to the great city of Rājagṛha."
"O virtuous ones!

If you know that this Tathāgata is on Vulture Peak Mountain, preaching the Dharma for the fourfold assembly—a teaching good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is subtle and exquisite, complete and pure, explaining the practice of the holy life."
"Therefore, you all should go to where the Tathāgata is; by doing so, you will achieve benefit and happiness for a long night.

At that time, the brahmins, kṣatriyas, elders, and householders of Rājagṛha, having been exhorted by Māra, took various incenses, flowers, unguents, powdered incense, burning incense, silk banners, precious parasols, robes, and other offerings, and departed from the great city of Rājagṛha, arriving at Vulture Peak Mountain.
Having prostrated with their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata, and having paid him respect, offered praise, made offerings, and shown reverence, they withdrew to stand to one side.

Māra Pāpīyān and his fourfold army emerged from the Great City of Rājagṛha and from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; having arrived where the Tathāgata was, they transformed themselves into celestial māndārava flowers which they scattered over the Buddha. Having scattered them, they and their fourfold army withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalanetra-suvimala-ratnacandraprabharāja saw Māra Pāpīyān sitting to one side and addressed him, saying: "Pāpīyān!
"For what reason have you brought these fourfold armies to the presence of the Tathāgata?
Māra replied,
"I have come here for the purpose of extinguishing this Dharma and for the purpose of harassing and disturbing the Tathāgata."
The Bodhisattva Vimalavaiśaradyaprabhāsa-ratnacandrarāja spoke to Māra Pāpīyān, saying: "Pāpīyān!
How can you trouble the Tathāgata and this Dharma?"
“Pāpīyan, you should now repent before the Tathāgata; do not bring about unbeneficial suffering and retribution for a long night.

After the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhāśuddharatnacandraprabha had delivered this teaching, Māra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and repented before the Tathāgata:
“May the World-Honored One accept my repentance!”

Out of ignorance, lack of wisdom, and lack of skillful means, I was unable to recognize my own state; thus, I gave rise to an evil mind in the presence of the Tathāgata and sought to destroy such sūtras as these.
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
Please grant me the formal acceptance of my confession and other such dharmas.
The Buddha spoke to the Māra Pāpīyan, saying:
"In my Dharma, one increases roots of goodness; that is to say, if a son or daughter of good family, desiring the purification of the Dharma, is now able to repent their transgressions."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas rose from his seat, stood before the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
You have previously established prohibitions against all afflictive unwholesome paths of action, such as harsh speech and the like.”
The Buddha said to Pāpīyas, “So it is,
so it is. Pāpīyas asked:
“The Tathāgata, the Lord of Dharma, for what reason addresses me by the name Pāpīyān?
The Buddha said, “Pāpīyān!”
I shall now provide an analogy.

Suppose there were an elder or a householder of great wealth, whose money and assets were inexhaustible; yet that person had only one son for whom he felt deep affection, regarding him as his very life upon which his own existence depended.
However, that only son was not well-disciplined and his mind was crooked and deceitful.

That elder and householder would treat him with their hands, a staff, or a whip, or else with harsh words and painful speech as a form of severe discipline, all for the sake of quelling his wickedness.
Pāpīyān! What do you think?
Would that householder or layman, out of anger and resentment, punish that one son?
He replied,
“World-Honored One!
It is solely for the sake of bringing that only son to maturity.”
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Pāpīyan! The Tathāgata is likewise."
Skillfully knowing the minds and mental factors of sentient beings, he speaks words of suffering and affliction to those who are to be tamed by such words;
to those who should be disciplined through ritual diagrams, he employs ritual diagrams;
and to those who should be gathered in, he speaks words of gathering.
Those who should be saved by means of a physical body, he saves them by means of a physical body;
those who should be saved by means of sound, fragrance, taste, touch, dharmas, and so forth, he saves them even by means of dharmas and so forth.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, having heard this Dharma from the Buddha, was filled with joy and exultation; he prostrated once more at the Buddha’s feet.
Having finished his prostration, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If there is anyone who preaches this Dharma within a village, town, or settlement, I shall go to that place for the sake of hearing this Dharma and to protect this sutra; furthermore, out of consideration for the benefit of the Dharma-preacher, many such auspicious signs will appear therein.

The assembly shall be tranquil and composed, free from frivolity, indolence, and the like; those who have attained the excellence of listening to the Dharma—whether reading, reciting, receiving and upholding, or explaining it—shall experience no physical fatigue and no mental weariness. Following this teaching as it is spoken, whether they listen to it or explain it extensively for others, they will thus give rise to a heart of increasing joy and exultation.

At that time, among that assembly there were various non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others; having seen and heard these words spoken by Māra the King, they immediately conceived a heart of joy and exultation toward the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what cause and by what condition do these various non-Buddhists, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, attain the realization of patience?”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In the past, on Vulture Peak Mountain in this city of Rājagṛha, there was a Buddha named Suvinīta-vijita Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who preached the Dharma."
After that Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma, various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) arrived with the intent to cause trouble.
Upon their arrival, they heard this teaching and immediately exclaimed, "Excellent!
yet they did not give rise to a heart of reverence toward the Buddha.

By the power of these causes and conditions, those non-Buddhists shall not be born among hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals for sixty thousand kalpas, but shall be born only in the realms of humans and devas.
Because those various non-Buddhists lack respect for the Tathāgata, they do not encounter virtuous spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in the places where they are reborn.
Ānanda, what do you think?
At that time, were those various non-Buddhist practitioners anyone else?
Ānanda! You should not conceive of them as being different.
Why is this? Good son! These various non-Buddhist followers of the Nirgranthas and others—
Ānanda! Now these various non-Buddhists have given rise to a heart of joy, reverence, and exultation toward the Tathāgata.
For this reason, the Tathāgata now prophesies that they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, when those non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others heard this prediction, their hearts leaped with great joy, and they immediately attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When this Dharma was being taught, twelve thousand people were freed from dust and removed of defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*).
Twenty thousand sentient beings who had never before resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* now gave rise to the aspiration for the Way.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this Dharma, read, recite, accept, uphold, and extensively explain it to others, how much merit will they obtain?
The Buddha said:
“If a good son or good daughter were to cause every single being in the realm of sentient beings, without exception, to dwell in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment)…”

Furthermore, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family reads, recites, accepts, and maintains this sutra, and explains it extensively for others, that person will obtain manifold merit and virtue.
Why is this? Ānanda!
This Dharma can cause one to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
“World-Honored One!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family conceives an evil mind toward this Dharma and the Dharma-preacher—
World-Honored One!”
"How much lack of benefit will those sons and daughters of good family incur?
The Buddha said,
"Sons of good family!"

If a son or daughter of good family were to gouge out the eyes of all sentient beings, yet another person were to give rise to an evil mind toward this Dharma and its teacher, that person would incur an evil retribution on account of this matter that is twice as great as the former.
Why is this? Ānanda!
This Dharma can provide illumination for all sentient beings.
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma should not be spoken before sons or daughters of good family who lack faith.”
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
It is because you should protect all sentient beings of future generations; do not preach this Dharma, lest they fall into the various hells due to the karmic retribution of slandering the Dharma.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“You should teach this Dharma. Why is that?”
"Those sentient beings, regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, take this very [teaching] as its cause.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"By what name is this sutra called,
and how should it be upheld?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"This sutra is titled 'The Ten Dharmas'; it should be upheld thus.
It is also titled 'The Inquiry of the Bodhisattva Vimalanirbhāsa-viśuddhi-ratnacandraprabharāja'; it should be upheld thus."

When the Tathāgata had spoken this Dharma, the Venerable Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Vimalanirmala-suvimala-ratnacandraprabharāja, along with the assembly of bodhisattvas, the assembly of bhikṣus, and the devas, humans, nāga kings, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Ten Dharmas of the Mahāyāna Spoken by the Buddha
